chapters.label: Intro
chapters.text: Happy Tuesday, it's November 24th. The Spurs are rolling, Nvidia's boss had a very short vacation, and the SEC is weighing whether to evict one of its own. Let's get into it.

chapters.label: 🏆 My Teams
chapters.text: Spurs first, because they earned it. San Antonio beat the Kings last night, 123 to 107, and they're now 15 and 3. Stephon Castle did a little of everything: 28 points, 8 rebounds and 11 assists. That's a near triple-double on a night when the game was never really in doubt. Fifteen and three. I'm just going to say that again and enjoy it.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket guy who runs Nvidia, has had quite a month. The BBC calls him the Taylor Swift of tech, which makes the news hit harder: allegations of two affairs, one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy. He resigned, and the story rattled the stock market. Eleven days later, the board put him back. They say he's the right person to lead the company, which is a confident read for a guy whose alleged pillow talk drew a counterintelligence angle. In fairness, Nvidia makes the chips that power basically all of the AI boom, so the board's priorities are visible from space. His fortune went from nearly two hundred billion dollars to around a hundred and five billion, so he's still doing fine. He's a Taiwan-born, Oregon State engineer who sold the American Dream and the family-man image for years. Now he gets to explain how that squares with a spy-adjacent love life.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: The SEC and LSU are in a full custody battle, and it's getting ugly. It started with LSU rostering RJ Luis, a former professional player, against conference rules. The SEC passed a penalty structure this summer, including a half-season coach suspension and fines up to half a sport's annual budget. Then it admitted in a court filing that it has no avenue to penalize LSU, because a Louisiana judge issued an injunction protecting the school. So the conference went for the one option the injunction doesn't cover. On December 3rd, two days before the SEC title game, the presidents and chancellors will meet to consider kicking LSU out entirely. It takes a two-thirds vote, and expulsion is still considered unlikely. But sources say enough of them are fed up that some might vote yes. When your punishment system collapses, you can always just try the door.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: Florida State has its guy. After a three-week search, the Seminoles hired Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann to replace Mike Norvell, who was fired November 1st at three and five. Norvell had won just ten games over three seasons, so fans were ready for anyone with a pulse and a plan. Schumann is thirty-six, has been with Kirby Smart since 2016, and runs the number six defense in the country, giving up 267 yards a game. He has never been a head coach. And he can't start yet, because Georgia is expected to be the top seed in the playoff, so he's busy trying to win a title for somebody else until at least late December. FSU's new coach doesn't show up until January. Tallahassee has seen long engagements, but this one's a bit much.

chapters.label: 💼 Business (light)
chapters.text: President Trump held another dinner for the top holders of his meme coin on Monday night, at his golf club in Northern Virginia. The pitch was the most exclusive dinner in the world. The more coin you hold, the closer you get to the president, and in the past plenty of attendees were from outside the U.S., which raises obvious influence questions. The White House denies any problem. The twist this time is the coin has cratered in price. One guest, crypto investor Morten Christensen, says a clever trading strategy meant he and his sister basically got in for free. They took an Uber. The most exclusive dinner in the world, and a guy rode up with his little sister and a coupon, essentially. It also lands as Democrats win majorities in Congress, which means the billions the Trump family has made in crypto will likely get investigated.

chapters.label: 💻 Tech
chapters.text: Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue SpaceX over Grok, the AI chatbot from Elon Musk's xAI, which SpaceX bought in February. The attorneys general say Grok is still generating sexualized images of real people, mostly women and children, including child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images. This follows the rollout of a Grok image feature Musk hyped, which turned out to generate a flood of that content, sometimes without being asked. Musk's companies apologized and said they'd added safeguards. The states call those claims misleading and say the company quietly embraced sexualized content to grab AI market share. X says every Grok output is screened. The complaint's main argument is that once these images exist, they can never be fully erased, and could resurface for a child's whole life. The states want to protect every user in their borders, which makes this one to watch.

chapters.label: 🌍 World
chapters.text: Three Russian cruise missiles landed in Poland on Friday. Nobody was hurt, but that's a NATO country, so the world noticed. The missiles hit a rural part of southeastern Poland, about thirty miles from the Ukrainian border, during one of Russia's biggest air attacks on Ukraine of the war. European forces were holding a military exercise in the region at the time. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it an intentional provocation. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte was in Germany today trying to reassure the alliance's eastern members, who have been warning for years that spillover was coming. Ukraine hit back over the weekend, with a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Baltic struck by what's suspected to be a Ukrainian sea drone. Kyiv also took credit for sinking a Russian warship in the Libyan port of Benghazi, thousands of miles from the front. Libya condemned it. The war keeps getting bigger on the map.

chapters.label: 🌍 World
chapters.text: Five days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the fallout is starting. The BBC says it's the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime. Britain just sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders and said it will pass legislation to cut off aviation fuel to the country. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said President Min Aung Hlaing, who was head of the military during the 2017 crackdown, is directly responsible for many of the atrocities. That crackdown killed thousands and forced more than seven hundred thousand Rohingya to flee. Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada also acknowledged the ruling. It also sets a precedent that could matter for the case over Israel's actions in Gaza.

chapters.label: ⚡ Quick hits
chapters.text: Quick hits. Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted prime minister, says she'll fly home from exile in India on December 16th, despite a death sentence handed down in her absence. The government says she can only come back through extradition, and she's expected to be arrested if she lands. The Pentagon issued an unusually blunt rebuke of Canada over defense spending and its review of American-made F-35 fighter jets, saying Canada must get serious. Malaysia says it will send more than sixty-five hundred Rohingya and other Myanmar refugees back to Myanmar next month, just days after that genocide ruling. And the first-ever Children's Booker Prize has its shortlist of eight books, with a fifty-thousand-pound prize and four kid judges who get a say. If the children don't love a book, it won't win, which is a standard most adult prizes could stand to adopt.

chapters.label: Wrapping up
chapters.text: That's your Tuesday. Go Spurs, stay skeptical of dinner invitations, and I'll catch you tomorrow.
